passage: It was a rushed evening and Aparna had only a few minutes before her bus to the night shift. Rukmini, five, pressed a crumpled paper rakhi into her hand. "For you. You're my Mama." Aparna crouched, tied it round her wrist and said, "Thank you. I'll wear it at work." Rukmini beamed and waved from the window as the bus pulled away.

qa.q: What did Rukmini press into Aparna's hand?
qa.a: A crumpled paper rakhi.

qa.q: What might Rukmini feel when Aparna ties it on so quickly?
qa.a: Pleased and loved, since she beamed and waved. She may also have wished for a little more time together.

qa.q: How does a warm reception like this teach a child?
qa.a: It shows that feelings can be shared through objects, even when the response is quick. 🤍

qa.q: How might Aparna feel with only a few minutes?
qa.a: Rushed but touched, since she stopped to crouch and tie it on.

grounding: Shows a preschooler pressing a handmade rakhi into a parent's hand to show affection, received warmly despite time pressure.

passage: After dinner in the flat, Shreya, five, pressed a folded drawing into her mother's hand. "For you. Because you made rotis even when you were tired." Manjula unfolded it: two smiling stick figures and a sun with a face. "Thank you, Shreya. I like the sun's smile." She stuck it on the almirah door. Shreya watched it go up, then ran off to draw another for Papa.

qa.q: Where did Manjula stick the drawing?
qa.a: On the almirah door.

qa.q: Why might Shreya have watched the drawing go up?
qa.a: She wants to see her gift valued, and to feel her thanks was received. She may also simply enjoy seeing it displayed.

qa.q: What did Manjula's response teach Shreya?
qa.a: That feelings can be shared through objects, and that a warm welcome encourages more.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel opening the drawing?
qa.a: Touched, and perhaps tired from the day. She smiled and put it where she would see it.

grounding: Shows a preschooler giving a drawing to say thank you, received warmly.

passage:
“Amma, close your eyes!”
Sangeeta closed them. Something papery was pushed into her hand.
“Open!”
It was a card, with a crooked flower glued on and a lot of glitter.
“I made it for you. Because you made me dosa.”
Sangeeta looked at it for a long moment. “Keerthana, this is beautiful. Thank you. It makes me so happy.”
“Really really?”
“Really really.” She stuck it on the fridge right away.
Keerthana did a little dance. “Tomorrow I'll make one for Appa.”

qa.q: Why did Keerthana make the card?
qa.a: Because Amma made her dosa.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she did a little dance?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy that her gift was received warmly, and grateful to Amma for the dosa.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta's warm response teach Keerthana?
qa.a: That feelings like thanks and love can be shared through things she makes, and that they matter.

qa.q: How might Appa feel tomorrow?
qa.a: He'd likely feel touched and happy to get a card too.

grounding: A preschooler gives her mother a handmade card to say thank you, and her mother receives it warmly.

passage:
Note from Sarika, nursery teacher.
Today at home time, Rashmi pressed a crumpled paper flower into my hand. She had made it in craft and saved it all day in her pocket. She said, “For you, because you helped me with my shoe.” I held it carefully, thanked her, and told her I'd put it on my desk. She watched to make sure I did. Her whole face lit up. It's small, but she's learning that she can share thanks through something she makes.

qa.q: Where had Rashmi kept the paper flower all day?
qa.a: In her pocket.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she watched to make sure Sarika put the flower on the desk?
qa.a: She felt hopeful and eager that her gift mattered, and her lit-up face showed she felt happy and proud.

qa.q: Why was it important for Sarika to receive the flower warmly?
qa.a: It taught Rashmi that her thanks and affection, shared through something she made, were valued.

qa.q: What would change if Sarika had tossed the crumpled flower aside?
qa.a: Rashmi would feel hurt and might stop sharing her feelings through gifts.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler giving a handmade flower in thanks, and the teacher receiving it warmly.

passage: In the village, Vijay Mama came back from the city for Diwali. Bhupen had waited all week. He pressed a paper star into Mama's hand, bright yellow with one bent point. “I made it. For you. So you don't forget us.” Vijay looked at the star, then at Bhupen. He crouched and tucked it carefully into his shirt pocket. “I'll keep it here, near my heart. I won't forget you.” Bhupen beamed and grabbed his hand to show him the goats.

qa.q: Where did Vijay Mama put the star?
qa.a: Into his shirt pocket.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when he gave the star?
qa.a: He felt affection and a little worry that Mama might forget them, and wanted to show love through his gift.

qa.q: What did Vijay Mama do that made the gift meaningful?
qa.a: He received it carefully, put it near his heart and promised not to forget, showing Bhupen his feelings mattered.

qa.q: How might Vijay Mama feel carrying the star back to the city?
qa.a: He'd likely feel loved and a bit homesick, with a reminder of Bhupen close by.

grounding: A preschooler gives his uncle a handmade paper star to show affection, and his uncle receives it warmly.

passage:
At the end of the day at the childminder's house in Durban, Sofia pressed a bead bracelet into Lindiwe's hand. It was lumpy, red and yellow, with the knot coming loose.

"I made it for you," Sofia said, looking at her shoes. "Because you helped me when I fell."

Lindiwe held it up to the light. "You made this? For me?" She slid it onto her wrist straight away. "It's beautiful. Thank you, Sofia."

Sofia looked up and beamed.

The next morning, Lindiwe was still wearing it. Sofia noticed immediately and pointed. "You kept it on!"

qa.q: What colours were the beads on the bracelet?
qa.a: Red and yellow.

qa.q: What was Sofia feeling when she looked at her shoes while giving the bracelet?
qa.a: She was most likely a little shy and hopeful, wanting Lindiwe to like her gift and to say thank you for the help. Her beaming afterwards shows she felt happy and proud.

qa.q: Why was putting the bracelet on straight away a good response?
qa.a: It received Sofia's gift warmly, showing her that her thanks and affection had reached Lindiwe.

qa.q: How is Lindiwe affected by the gift?
qa.a: She seems touched by it, praising it and still wearing it the next morning.

grounding: It shows a preschooler giving a handmade bracelet to show gratitude and affection, and an adult receiving it warmly.
